title: The circulatory system
text:
The circulatory system moves blood around the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste. It consists of the heart, the blood vessels and the blood itself. The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two atria on top and two ventricles below. A wall of muscle called the septum separates the left side of the heart from the right side.

Blood that has given up its oxygen returns to the right atrium through large veins. The right atrium pushes the blood into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Oxygen-rich blood then returns to the left atrium. The left ventricle, which has the thickest walls, pumps the blood out through the aorta to the rest of the body. Valves between the chambers open and close to keep blood flowing in one direction.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls. Veins carry blood back to the heart and contain valves that prevent backflow. Capillaries are tiny vessels with walls only one cell thick, which lets oxygen and nutrients pass into tissues. Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries.

The sinoatrial node, a small group of cells in the right atrium, sets the rhythm of the heartbeat. It sends out electrical signals that make the atria contract, and then the ventricles. Exercise raises the heart rate so that muscles receive more oxygen. High blood pressure forces the heart to work harder and can damage the arteries over time. Red blood cells carry oxygen using a protein called haemoglobin. White blood cells and platelets are also carried in the blood.

title: From DNA to protein
text:
DNA stores the instructions for building a cell's proteins in the order of its four bases. The bases are adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine, and adenine pairs with thymine while guanine pairs with cytosine. DNA has the shape of a double helix, with two strands wound around each other. Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied in a process called replication.

In replication, an enzyme called helicase unwinds and separates the two strands. DNA polymerase then builds a new strand along each old strand by adding matching bases. Each new DNA molecule therefore contains one old strand and one new strand. Proofreading by DNA polymerase keeps errors very rare, but mutations still occur occasionally.

Making a protein begins with transcription, in which a section of DNA is copied into messenger RNA. The enzyme RNA polymerase reads the DNA and builds the mRNA using the base uracil in place of thymine. In eukaryotes the mRNA is then processed and leaves the nucleus. In the cytoplasm, a ribosome attaches to the mRNA and begins translation. Transfer RNA molecules bring amino acids to the ribosome, each matching a three-base codon on the mRNA. The ribosome joins the amino acids in order to form a chain. The chain folds into a protein with a specific shape.

The genetic code is the set of rules that links each codon to an amino acid. Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. A mutation that changes a codon can alter the amino acid and therefore the protein. Some mutations have no effect, while others cause diseases such as sickle cell anaemia. Cells control which genes are transcribed, so different cell types make different proteins.

title: The life cycle of stars
text:
Stars form inside enormous clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Gravity pulls the material in a region of the cloud together into a dense clump. As the clump contracts it heats up, and it becomes a protostar. When the core reaches about ten million degrees, hydrogen nuclei begin to fuse into helium, and the star is born.

A star spends most of its life on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. The energy released by fusion produces outward pressure that balances the inward pull of gravity. A star's mass determines how long this stage lasts. Massive stars burn their fuel quickly and live for only millions of years, while small stars can last for trillions. The Sun is a medium-sized star and has been on the main sequence for about five billion years.

When the hydrogen in the core runs out, fusion slows and gravity makes the core contract. The outer layers expand and cool, and the star becomes a red giant. A star like the Sun then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula. The hot core that remains is a white dwarf, which slowly cools over billions of years.

A star much more massive than the Sun ends in a violent explosion called a supernova. The supernova scatters heavy elements such as iron and carbon into space. If the remaining core is very massive it collapses into a neutron star. If it is more massive still, it collapses into a black hole, whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape. The gas and dust from dead stars later become part of new nebulae. In this way the elements in our bodies were made inside earlier stars. Astronomers classify stars by their colour, temperature and brightness.

title: Supply and demand
text:
In a market, the price of a good is set by the interaction of supply and demand. Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers want at each price. The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price lowers the quantity demanded. Supply is the quantity that sellers are willing to offer at each price. The law of supply says that a higher price raises the quantity supplied.

The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. If the price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, and a surplus appears. A surplus pushes sellers to cut prices until the market clears. If the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer, and a shortage appears. A shortage lets sellers raise prices until supply and demand balance.

Demand can shift when incomes change, when tastes change or when the price of a related good changes. A rise in demand moves the demand curve to the right and raises the equilibrium price and quantity. Supply can shift when production costs change or when technology improves. A fall in production costs moves the supply curve to the right, which lowers the equilibrium price and raises the quantity.

Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to a change in price. Necessities such as salt have inelastic demand because people buy about the same amount whatever the price. Luxuries tend to have elastic demand because buyers can easily go without them. A price ceiling set below equilibrium creates a persistent shortage.

title: How data crosses the internet
text:
Data sent across the internet is broken into small units called packets. Each packet carries part of the message together with the addresses of the sender and the receiver. Packets from the same message can travel by different routes and are put back in order when they arrive. Breaking data into packets lets many users share the same links efficiently.

Every device on the internet is identified by an IP address. Routers are devices that forward packets toward their destination. A router reads the destination address of each packet and chooses the next link to send it along. Routers exchange information with each other so that they know which paths are available. If a link fails, routers can send packets along another path.

The Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, makes the connection reliable. TCP numbers each packet so that the receiver can detect missing or out-of-order packets. The receiver sends acknowledgements, and the sender retransmits any packet that is not acknowledged. The User Datagram Protocol, or UDP, skips these checks and is faster but less reliable. Video calls often use UDP because a late packet is worth less than a delay.

The Domain Name System translates website names into IP addresses. When you type a web address, your computer asks a DNS server for the matching IP address. The DNS server may ask other servers if it does not already know the answer. Your browser then opens a connection to that address and requests the page. Web servers reply with the page, which arrives as a stream of packets. Encryption protects the contents of packets so that others cannot read them in transit.

title: The French Revolution
text:
The French Revolution began in 1789 and transformed French society. Before it, France was ruled by an absolute monarchy, and society was divided into three estates. The clergy formed the first estate and the nobility the second, and both paid few taxes. The third estate, made up of everyone else, bore most of the tax burden.

By the 1780s the state was close to bankruptcy because of wars and court spending. A poor harvest in 1788 raised the price of bread and increased hunger in the cities. King Louis XVI called the Estates General in 1789 to approve new taxes. The third estate demanded more power and declared itself the National Assembly. On 14 July 1789 a crowd stormed the Bastille, a prison that symbolised royal power.

In August 1789 the Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The Declaration stated that men are born free and equal in rights. The Assembly abolished feudal privileges and, later, reorganised the Church under state control. In 1791 a constitution made France a constitutional monarchy.

In 1792 war with Austria and Prussia radicalised the revolution, and the monarchy was abolished. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. The Committee of Public Safety, led by Robespierre, then ruled during the Reign of Terror. Tens of thousands of people were executed or died in prison during the Terror. Robespierre fell in July 1794, and a more moderate government, the Directory, followed. In 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup. The revolution spread ideas of citizenship and equality across Europe.
